title: Decoupled domain-texture switching from magnetic easy axis in kagome ferromagnet EuTi3Bi4
authors: Yunhao Wang, Shiyu Zhu, Guohao Xi, Runnong Zhou, Ruwen Wang, Jianfeng Guo, Jiali Liu, Zichao Chen, Kailin Xu, Cong Wang, Chengmin Shen, Jiang Xiao, Haitao Yang, Xiaoli Dong, Wei Ji, Hong-Jun Gao
abstract: Magnetic anisotropy defines the easy axis of a magnetic material and governs the spatial arrangement of its domains. To date, anisotropy engineering has focused on reorienting the easy axis or tuning the anisotropy energy, both of which demand substantial energy input. Here, we demonstrate that magnetic domain textures can be switched without reorienting the easy axis, as observed in a kagome ferromagnet EuTi3Bi4 crystal. Using low-temperature magnetic force microscopy, we observe that the preferred orientation of magnetic domains switches from the a-axis to the b-axis upon temperature variation, and that this switching can also be triggered by an out-of-plane magnetic-field reset. Magnetization measurements and density functional theory calculations confirm a robust c-axis easy magnetization, ruling out a conventional spin-reorientation transition. Instead, the texture switching is governed by the temperature dependence of the in-plane variation of the Magnetic anisotropy energy landscape, which arises from two competing interactions with different decay rates: single-ion anisotropy favors a-oriented spin components, while nearest-neighbor anisotropic exchange favors b-oriented ones. Furthermore, the critical switching temperature is substantially elevated in a mechanically exfoliated EuTi3Bi4 flake. Our findings establish that macroscopic magnetic textures can be effectively manipulated by tuning the competition between in-plane anisotropic interactions, without the energy cost of reorienting the easy axis.
summary: This work reports on a novel mechanism for controlling magnetic domain textures in the kagome ferromagnet $	ext{EuTi}_3	ext{Bi}_4$. By combining MFM and DFT, the authors show that the domain orientation switches between the a- and b-axes purely due to temperature changes. This switching is governed by the competition between two anisotropic exchange interactions, demonstrating a low-energy pathway for magnetic control without altering the primary easy axis direction.
main_problem: The research addresses how magnetic domain textures can be switched in a ferromagnet without requiring the high energy input associated with reorienting the material's magnetic easy axis.
main_result: They demonstrate that the domain texture switching in $	ext{EuTi}_3	ext{Bi}_4$ is governed by the temperature-dependent competition between single-ion anisotropy (favoring a-axis) and nearest-neighbor anisotropic exchange (favoring b-axis).
method: The study combines low-temperature magnetic force microscopy (MFM) to observe domain patterns, magnetization measurements, and Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations to model the underlying magnetic anisotropy energy landscape.
model_or_system: The physical system is the kagome ferromagnet $	ext{EuTi}_3	ext{Bi}_4$. The magnetic anisotropy energy landscape is modeled by considering the competition between single-ion anisotropy and anisotropic exchange interactions, which dictates the in-plane domain preference.
key_observables: Magnetic domain orientation (switching between a-axis and b-axis), the ratio $R_a = I_a / (I_a + I_b)$, and the critical switching temperature ($T_s$).
important_parameters: Temperature (T), applied magnetic field ($B$), and the relative strengths of the single-ion anisotropy ($A$) and anisotropic exchange ($J$) interactions.
main_assumptions: The switching mechanism is attributed solely to the temperature dependence of the in-plane anisotropic interactions, ruling out conventional spin-reorientation transitions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature-dependent domain switching via MFM images and $R_a$ vs $B_z$ curves, while DFT calculations confirm the c-axis as the global easy axis, showing the competition between $A$ and $J$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by noting the difficulty of anisotropy engineering, presents experimental evidence of in-plane texture switching in $	ext{EuTi}_3	ext{Bi}_4$, and then uses DFT and theoretical modeling to attribute this switching to the temperature-dependent competition between two specific anisotropic exchange terms.
why_interesting: The concept of manipulating macroscopic magnetic textures via tuning the competition between competing anisotropic interactions, rather than changing the easy axis, offers a highly tunable and potentially low-energy control mechanism relevant to advanced spintronics.
